INTRODUCTION TO PROGRAMMING
w Explain the purpose and usage of programming a microprocessor system.
w Understand the different types of programming and what type the Nida 68000 microprocessor trainer uses.
w Define the different groups of instructions and which instructions are in those groups.
w Observe and understand all of the instruction code of a simple program.
w Observe the effects of executing the simple program...............................
OBJECTIVES
. The experiment in this lesson is not setup to use the selected trainer.

Definition

Understanding programming is for more than just computer science or software engineering people. Electrical and Computer engineers along with technicians need to know how programming works to understand the operation of a microprocessor performing certain tasks.

In this lesson, four aspects of programming will be covered in the following order: First we will look at why programming is necessary, followed by a look at the different methods of programming and what method the 68000 microprocessor trainer uses.

Next, we will look at the different programming instruction groups and what instructions are in each group. Finally, an experiment will explain, in detail, a small program and ask you to enter the program to validate its description.
Let's begin the lesson on INTRODUCTION TO PROGRAMMING.....................
LESSON MENU
Why programming? Without programs a microprocessor is useless. Programs are what allow a microprocessor to perform operations. Without them it would just sit and do nothing.
I NEED PROGRAMS!
DISCUSSION
To understand programming you need to look at the situations in which programming will be performed. Programming may be divided into two main categories, system and user programs.
PROGRAMSAMS
PROGRAMSS
System programs are normally designed by engineers involved in the creation of a microprocessor system. These programs handle error detections and system management.
PROGRAMS
PROGRAMSAMS

These are programs that cannot afford to have errors, and are normally checked multiple times by many different people. The monitor program on the 68000 microprocessor or an operating system is an example of a system program.
PROGRAMSAMS
PROGRAMS
Average programmers do not have the knowledge to write such elaborate segments of code. Once a system has been designed, like a microcomputer, applications are written for the system.
PROGRAMSAMS
These programs can be called user programs, and are written by all types of people, including engineers, technicians and even students.
PROGRAMS
User programs allow you to use certain portions of the system programs and allow you to create your own routines for performing certain tasks.
PROGRAMS
While you may use a system program or routine to access a serial port, the system program has no clue about what type of information is being read from the serial port.
PROGRAMS

User programs can perform routines on the information since the user knows which device is attached to the serial port. It may even be a device the user created, meaning the system programmer would have no knowledge of the new device in most cases.
PROGRAMS
As a technician, you may create some programs to run through a specific pattern of events for testing system operation.
In another scenario, a technician may want to modify a few of the parameters of a routine written by an engineer.
What type of program is normally created by a technician to test certain sections of operation in the microprocessor system?
System programs are normally designed by highly qualified programmers to perform basic level tasks pertinent to system operation. A user program would be used for this task, not a system program.
TRY AGAIN!
Programming is divided into three categories of languages: low-level programming, high-level programming, and natural programming. Let's look at each of these.
Low-level programming is the most basic form of programming. Assembly language and machine language programming fall into this category.

This programming method is very repetitive, difficult to understand and closely resembles the actual operation of the microprocessor. You will be programming the microprocessor in machine language like you have been doing in previous lessons.
Machine language programming is probably the most difficult to perform, however, it provides the most educational benefit for understanding the system as it operates.
It is important to note that all other programming techniques will convert their code to machine language since this is what the microprocessor operates with.

Assembly language programming is the next step up from machine language programming in the low-level programming group. Assembly language is performed by creating a text file containing instructions with parameters.

In the previous lesson you could see the assembly language next to the machine language code that you were entering. Assembly language allows you to add comments and be a bit more descriptive in the operation of code.
Each instruction name gives you some insight into the operation it is performing. When assembly code is ready to be used it is normally compiled into machine code.

To compile is to examine the assembly language code and generate the appropriate machine language code. Normally, if errors are found, the compiler can be instructed to produce a list file showing the errors that were created.
The chart below shows an assembly language file..............
ASSEMBLY CODE
MOVE.A.L #DATA,A0
ASSEMBLY LANGUAGE
This is the List File showing Assembly Code Error..........
MOVE.A.L #DATA,A0
ASSEMBLY LANGUAGE
EXPLANATION

There are two important issues to look at here. First, there are many different assembly compilers which may differ slightly in format. Second, assembly language is restricted to the microprocessor or family of microprocessors.
This is a disadvantage to programming in low-level; however, you have the advantage of complete control of your code with an assurance of what exactly will occur.
Programs written for the 68000 microprocessor are upwards compatible, meaning they will run on later editions in the series of this processor, like the 68020, 68030, 68040 and so on.
High-level programming is the next level of programming. This is the most popular method today. There are many different types of high-level languages like C, C++, Pascal, Fortran, Lisp, Java, etc.
The list goes on and on, each with their own advantages and disadvantages. High-level languages are not programmed with the instructions of the actual processor.

General functions are created and used which are converted into machine code by the compiler of the language. The advantage is that this method of explaining code allows it to be compiled on different compilers.

In high-level languages the compilers can become very complex and allow little work by the programmer compared to a low-level language. The disadvantage is that actual program operation may be unknown.

The compiler chooses how to implement the function you define. This can cause code to be slower or larger than if it were written in assembly. Most advanced high-level programming language compilers offer options to compile code in certain ways.
Most high-level languages are developed for microcomputer systems that will be mass produced.
The last type of programming technique is the natural programming language. This type of programming, currently, doesn't fully exist. However, some high-level languages are getting close.
Natural programming allows the programmer to write his program in a natural language like English. For example a command could be "move the register contents of A0 into the accumulator and add 5".
While this may appear straight forward, there are often varied interpretations of words or phrases, making English and other natural languages too ambiguous.
This area of programming is constantly being worked and will be implemented in the years to come.
Which of the following programming languages is known as a high-level programming language?
The language you have selected is from the low-level programming language group of languages.
TRY AGAIN!
Now that you are aware of the different techniques of programming, let's look at the type of programing you will be performing. All explanation of code will be in its assembly language counterpart.

When you enter the code into the microprocessor trainer you will enter the machine code which will be provided for you. The conversion of machine code to assembly and assembly to machine code will be explained in the next few lessons.
There are 76 pre-defined instructions separated into 6 different categories: logic commands, test commands, branch commands, move commands, arithmetic commands and additional commands.
DFB "Port",0ort",0 "Port",0FB "Port",0FB "Parallel"
ARITHMETIC
ADDITIONAL

The undefined instructions, also known as unimplimented instructions, are not discussed because these macro instructions are created by the system programmer or even the user programmer, depending on the system.
Each of the instructions of these groups will be covered in detail in the following lessons. In this lesson we will look at a description of each group and what instructions are within that group.
Logic commands are used to perform bit and decision making functions. Logic functions include AND, OR, NOT, Logic Shift Left, etc.
DFB "Port",0ort",0 "Port",0FB "Port",0FB "Parallel"
You are probably familiar with these types of operations from digital electronics. You first learned a practical use of logic commands when we discussed masking bits in an earlier lesson.
You will see how logic commands can perform certain types of operations, and combined with other operations, to perform many different types of functions.
Remember that the arithmetic instructions are created from sequences of logic operations and packaged into a single instruction.
Test commands allow you to perform some sort of test on a given condition and act accordingly. Different types of test commands are; Test a bit, Test a bit and set, etc.
DFB "Port",0ort",0 "Port",0FB "Port",0FB "Parallel"
Test commands are important when only isolated information is needed. A test command could check a single bit of the status register and allow you to know what that value was.
With the exception of the additional commands, test commands are not used as often as most other commands.
These types of instructions are important since different types of conditions arise in programs where different actions will need to occur for different values.
DFB "Port",0ort",0 "Port",0FB "Port",0FB "Parallel"
ARITHMETIC
ADDITIONAL
Branch commands include: Branch, if Z in status register is set, Decrement and branch, if N bit in status register is clear, Branch to certain location, etc.

Loops are constructed with branch commands. A register is set to a certain value and decremented each time through the loop. A branch command can see if the value is equal to zero and, if so, exit out of the loop.
This is a very common method of looping. Remember, looping is a term used to describe the repetitious execution of code.

Care must be taken when creating loops to avoid infinite loops which are considered a program bug. You will quickly become aware of the importance of branching instructions. They allow algorithms to be created very easily.
In programming an algorithm is a piece of code designed to perform a specific function. Suppose you want to make a program that converts Celsius to Fahrenheit.
You would create an algorithm (piece of code) that would take an input (the Celsius temperature) and output a result (a Fahrenheit temperature). Algorithms vary in size and complexity.
Some perform error checking and some don't. The term algorithm is very similar to the term function, just more defined in its operation.
It is important to note that some of the branching instructions also incorporate testing.
Of all the groups we have mentioned, you have probably seen move instructions more than anything else in the previous lesson's experiments.
DFB "Port",0ort",0 "Port",0FB "Port",0FB "Parallel"
ARITHMETIC
ADDITIONAL

Moving is one of the most common instructions performed. Data is moved in, passed through algorithms, and then returned. There are many different varieties of the move command for different data sizes.

The most important aspect of the move command is the different addressing modes for the data being moved. As you progress through this lesson, you will learn more about various move commands and the modes of addressing they interface with.
Arithmetic commands are exactly what their name implies. Because Microprocessors understand only numbers (specifically binary) math in some form is used for every function performed.
Whether it is simulations for engineers, financial data for home use, or even repositioning items on the screen, math is involved in performing the tasks.

All of the basic arithmetic functions have been implemented into the system. Some instructions are also provided for BCD data. Remember, BCD data is another form of encoding numerical values into a microprocessor.

Information on BCD can be found in Lesson 1 of the 68000 microprocessor lessons. Arithmetic instructions perform the functions of addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, shifting, negating, etc.
There are also many variations of each of these, which individually provide advantages and/or disadvantages over other instructions.
Additional commands are those that had specialized functions that can not be classified as a part of the other groups.
Some of these are used frequently, like CLR (Clear) which can clear data in a register, memory location, etc. Others include: Load Effective Address, Link and Allocate, Push Effective Address etc.
You will see that some of the additional instructions are very useful, while others have more limited applications.
Arithmetic instructions comprise the largest of the groups. However, many commands are the same commands in different variations.
DFB "Port",0ort",0 "Port",0FB "Port",0FB "Parallel"
ARITHMETIC
ADDITIONAL

People are often overwhelmed when first confronted with programming. In programming, there is not a single solution for any given task. Programming is an art which takes many years to develop and fine tune.
In the next few lessons you will learn about these commands, see them in example code, and use them in application.
You will not be required to completely write a program. This would be very difficult for people with little or no programming experience.

Don't be dissuaded, however, from trying to write your own simple program. Use the examples in the book. Programming is a learn-by-doing process. You will probably have a lot of fun writing your own code.
The number of people actually programming in assembly and machine language will decrease over the years. Descriptive programming techniques are used more often than those more functionally vague.
Companies and organizations don't want ambiguous languages. That is why the Department of Defense developed their ADA programming language, an efficient language that is well defined.

Earlier, we mentioned how programs for the 68000 can be executed on later editions of the microprocessor. This is not true in every case. The instruction sets become larger and larger as you move up the versions of the 68000 family.

Different features like memory management and co-processors require the use of additional functions. The purpose of the upward compatibility is to keep current programs compatible with newer chip sets.

If they weren't, people would be reluctant to buy them, knowing all of their current software would not be usable. In the next section you will be performing an experiment on programming the 68000 microprocessor.
This completes the information on INTRODUCTION TO PROGRAMMING.

2. The two types of programs are system and user programs. The three types of programming languages are; low-level, high-level and natural language programming.

3. The microprocessor only understands machine language. All other programming methods must compile their code into machine language.
4. The advantage of machine language is complete control and optimization of a program. The disadvantage is readability.
5. There are a total of 76 instructions with a variety of combinations of parameters, in the instruction set of the 68000 CPU.
DFB "Port",0ort",0 "Port",0FB "Port",0FB "Parallel"

6. Instructions are classified into the following groups: Logic, Test, Branch, Move, Arithmetic and Additional commands.

EXPERIMENT
After this, you will be asked to enter and test it on the 68000 microprocessor trainer. Let's begin the experiment.
1. Set the Test Console controls to the initial control settings..........

2. Carefully insert the PC130-468 card into the PC1 position, the PC130-403 card into the PC2 position, the PC130-401 card into the PC3 position and place the PC130-404 card in front of the test console.
3. Set the Positive Supply Voltage to 5 volts.............................
4. Using the 50-pin short cable, connect PC1 J1 and PC2 J2 together. Remember to align the red edge cable with the end of the connector labled either 1 or 2.
5. Using the 20-pin short cable, connect PC2 J2 and PC3 J1 together. Remember to align the red edge cable with the end of the connector labled either 1 or 2.
6. Using the 20-pin long cable, connect PC3 J2 and the Keyboard and Display J1 together. Remember to align the red edge cable with the end of the connector labled either 1 or 2.
The program below shows the code that we will examine. Line numbers are provided on each line of the code to easily identify the instruction we are talking about.
ASSEMBLY LANGUAGE
MOVEA.L #1101EH,A0
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS

You probably recognize this code to be the same program used in Lesson 5. The purpose of using a familiar program is that you have seen how it works. You can make predictions of how the code is supposed to operate.
This will help in the understanding of each operation. The first line of code is a trap instruction. In Lesson 5, you learned that traps are used to call subroutines built into the system.
MOVEA.L #1101EH,A0
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS

The particular subroutine that we are calling clears the screen of the LCD display unit. If you look through the previous experiments in which the #0H trap is used, you'll note its presence whenever the display module is used.
You would not write text to a screen that is filled with other information. When the processor evaluates this instruction, it handles the trap instruction as an exception.

It loads an address stored in a vector table and executes a program associated to that trap number. An RTE inside the trap program will return you to the next instruction after the trap instruction of the program.
Remember that RTE is return from exception. It pulls the value of the status register and the value of the program counter and places them into the associated registers.
The next instruction, line 2, is MOVE.L #0101H,D0. In this instruction we move the immediate data of #0101H into data register D0. The .L indicates that we want to move a longword into D0.
MOVEA.L #1101EH,A0
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS
Since 0101H is word sized, the other word of the longword will be replaced with zeros. If the .L had been a .W, the other word in the data register would have remained unchanged.
The value 0101H is being loaded for the next instruction, which is another trap. Trap routines may need parameters, like a size, a memory address, etc.

To pass these values to the trap you could put them on the stack or place them in a pre-defined register. The traps used in this 68000 microprocessor trainer look for values placed in pre-defined registers.
The value passed is actually an X,Y position. X is 01 and Y is 01. Instruction 3, TRAP #0CH is used to position the cursor on the screen based on the X and Y values stored in D0.
ASSEMBLY LANGUAGE
MOVEA.L #1101EH,A0
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS
The trap routine takes the values in D0 and places the cursor at that location. The number sign in front of the value, like the two previous instructions, indicates immediate values.
In other terms, the value used in the operation is that of the one following the number sign. If the number sign wasn't there, the data at the address location of that value would be used.

This is known as Indirect addressing. Addressing modes will be covered in more detail in later lessons. The 0 before the C is a restriction of the compiler. If we just had a CH the compiler would think that this is a label....
We want it to represent a hexadecimal number. The zero tells the compiler that this is a value not a label. The H just after the number indicates the hexadecimal numbering system.
The compiler assumes decimal if no letter is there. A label is used to represent a location. In assembly language, labels make branching much easier.
The 4th instruction, MOVEA.L #1101EH,A0 loads the address value into A0 where text is stored to be displayed on the screen. Notice the A in the move command.
MOVEA.L #1101EH,A0
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS

This is a special move command for loading address registers with information. This value will be used by the trap command on line 5. The text for the command on line 9 (No Exception Called, 0) has been divided and placed on lines 10 and 11, also.
This is so that the machine code can fit on one page. Notice that the last of the text ends with a zero. The trap command uses this zero to indicate the end of text.
The next instruction, line 5, is the TRAP #0AH. This trap uses the address value in A0 and displays text at that location until a byte sized value of zero is found.
ASSEMBLY LANGUAGE
MOVEA.L #1101EH,A0
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS

If the zero wasn't there, whatever was next in memory would fill the screen until a zero was found in memory. Line 6 contains another move address command. This loads the value #00010000H into the Address Register A0.
MOVEA.L #1101EH,A0
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS

The purpose for this instruction and the next instruction was used in the previous lesson to demonstrate an illegal address privilege exception. If the address value was odd, like #00010003H, the next instruction would cause the exception.

The next instruction loads the value stored at the location pointed at by A0 into the D0 register. This is known as indirect addressing. The value of A0 is not put into D0. Rather, AO points to a memory address and the value stored at that address is loaded into DO.
MOVEA.L #1101EH,A0
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS

The Branch instruction on line 8 branches back to line 6. This prevents the program from ending. Normally, this condition would not be desired in a microprocessor system because the program would never end.
MOVEA.L #1101EH,A0
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS
When programs terminate correctly on the 68000 trainer, a message is displayed on the screen. If we let this program terminate correctly you wouldn't see the output to the display by the program.

The text isn't necessary to explain since we know that it just allows us to store data in memory. The DFB allows us to store sequential byte sized data. It can be entered as strings like "Hello" or separated with commas 5,6,255.
MOVEA.L #1101EH,A0
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS
You can even put a combination like 5,"Hello",128. DFB is not a command of the 68000, but a command of the assembler. Other assemblers use DC.B to perform the same action.
Many assembly language compilers have their own conventions. It is important to always read the documentation before using.

Now that we have gone through the above code you should have a better understanding of how it works. Enter in the code and begin the program. The program should show that it operates with the described actions.
1. Press the Reset key on the PC130-468 card. The main screen of the monitor program should be displayed.

2. Press the EDIT key and enter the value "11000". Enter the code shown in Program 1. Remember to be careful when entering in the values. For more help on entering programs, refer to the experiment in lesson 3 or see your instructor for assistance.
3. Once you have finished entering the code, press the STOP key, press the RUN key on the 68000 keypad and enter the address value "11000". Press ENTER.
Observe the display of the 68000. There should be the words "No Exception Called" just as was described in the program description.
Now that you know how it works, you may want to look at the ASCII table and change the text displayed. You know where the text starts, just don't forget to end the text with a zero.
Without the zero, garbled text will be displayed on the 68000 trainer.

The purpose for this instruction and the next instruction was used in the previous lesson to demonstrate an illegal address privilege exception. If the address value was odd, like #00010003H, the next instruction would cause the exception.

The next instruction loads the value stored at the location pointed at by A0 into the D0 register. This is known as indirect addressing. The value of A0 is not put into D0. Rather, AO points to a memory address and the value stored at that address is loaded into DO.
MOVEA.L #1101EH,A0
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS

The Branch instruction on line 8 branches back to line 6. This prevents the program from ending. Normally, this condition would not be desired in a microprocessor system because the program would never end.
MOVEA.L #1101EH,A0
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS
When programs terminate correctly on the 68000 trainer, a message is displayed on the screen. If we let this program terminate correctly you wouldn't see the output to the display by the program.

The text isn't necessary to explain since we know that it just allows us to store data in memory. The DFB allows us to store sequential byte sized data. It can be entered as strings like "Hello" or separated with commas 5,6,255.
MOVEA.L #1101EH,A0
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS
You can even put a combination like 5,"Hello",128. DFB is not a command of the 68000, but a command of the assembler. Other assemblers use DC.B to perform the same action.
Many assembly language compilers have their own conventions. It is important to always read the documentation before using.
